pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 10. Bowls sold: 23. Bowls spilled: 4. Bowls praised: 1.*

The burner sputtered. The flame died with a soft *phut*, leaving only the smell of unburnt gas. I flicked the switch again. It popped back to life, roaring like a startled cat.

"Not so much gas," Ama said from her plastic stool, her wrist wrapped in white tape. "More."

She said both things in the same breath. I stood there, turning the knob left, then right, feeling like a pilot trying to land a plane in a hurricane. Uncle Feng, who was passing by with a tray of oyster omelets, stopped. He looked at the pot, then at me. With a grunt that vibrated through his forearms, he reached down and lifted the heavy steel lid, letting the steam escape in a long, white sigh.

I tied my red-and-white checked apron around my waist. I pulled it tight. Then I tied it again, just to be sure. It turned out that was one time too many. The knot sat high on my lower back, uncomfortable and tight, but it felt like armor. I adjusted my pencil behind my ear. The market was waking up.
pages.image: Lin, a small girl with a black bob and green jacket, ties a red-and-white apron twice while Uncle Feng, a round man in a bandana, lifts a heavy steel lid from a steaming pot in the background.

pages.text:
The first family arrived, five of them, carrying the scent of cold air and high expectations. Behind them stood a man in a crisp suit, checking his watch with the impatience of someone waiting for a bus. My hands went numb. I reached for the noodles, but my brain had forgotten the step. I dropped the bundle into the pot too early. They turned into a gluey, trembling lump that looked like a mistake I had made in a math test.

I ladled the soup, but my hand shook so badly the bowl tipped, sending a splash of dark broth onto the man’s shiny shoe. I grabbed the sugar jar, my fingers clumsy, and dumped a spoonful into the pot instead of the salt shaker.

From her chair, Ama did not shout. She just sniffed the air, her nose twitching once.

"Taste, Lin," she said quietly.

I dipped my finger in. It was sweet. It was wrong. I wanted to sink into the broth and disappear. The man in the suit looked at his shoe, then at me, and walked away. The family sat down, but they did not order.
pages.image: Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, stares nervously at a bowl of soup on a tray while a man in a dark suit sits on a plastic stool looking at his wet shoe; Ama with silver curls watches calmly from behind the pot.

pages.text:
By eight o'clock, four bowls had been spilled. Twenty-three were sold. The queue that had formed at seven was mostly gone, leaving only a thin line of hesitant faces who glanced at our empty tables and moved on to the oyster omelet stall.

I turned my face to the wall where the steam was thickest. It was the only place in the market where nobody could see my eyes. I breathed in the star anise, trying to keep my face still. I was not crying. I was just sweating. Probably.

A voice, soft and familiar, cut through the steam.

"Lin?"

Hui-Ting was standing at table two. She wore her glasses and her two long braids. Beside her stood her grandmother, a quiet woman in a gray coat. Hui-Ting's grandmother did not say a word. She simply sat down on the plastic stool, folded her hands in her lap, and waited patiently to be sad on my behalf.
pages.image: Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, turns her face toward the steam at a night-market stall while her tall friend Hui-Ting with glasses and two long braids in a purple cardigan stands beside an elderly woman in a gray coat sitting at a small table.

pages.text:
Old Mr. Gao arrived late, his straw hat tilted low over his eyes. He was the shrimp-fishing man, the one who told jokes so bad they made you want to hold your ears. He slid onto a stool and ordered his usual.

When the bowl arrived, he did not eat immediately. He slurped. He paused. He slurped again. His eyes were closed, and his lips moved slightly, as if he were counting something.

"Tastes like your Ama," he said finally, opening one eye. "A little slower."

I felt a pang of hurt. "That is not a compliment," I said, wiping a speck of broth from the counter.

Mr. Gao laughed, a dry, rattling sound. At his age, he said, being a little slower was the best compliment there was. It meant the soup had time to think. He finished the last drop, leaving the bowl empty and shiny.
pages.image: An old man in a straw hat slurps from a bowl while Lin, a small girl in a checked apron, watches with a worried expression; steam rises between them in the warm light. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
The last customer left, taking the cold air with him. The lane was quiet, save for the hum of the refrigerators and the distant laughter from the bubble tea stall. I stood by the counter, my arms aching from carrying bowls.

Ama stood up. She walked over to the shelf where the tools hung. She took down the old brass ladle. It was dented, the handle worn smooth by decades of hands. It had been her mother’s. She handed it to me. It was warm from the pot.

I took it. My fingers curled around the handle. It was heavy, but it felt right in my grip.

"Again tomorrow," Ama said. She did not smile, but she nodded.

I opened the red ledger. I picked up my pencil. I wrote the number 23. It was the worst number I had ever written. And it was the one I was proudest of.
pages.image: Lin, a small girl with a black bob, holds a dented brass ladle while her grandmother, a small woman with silver curls, watches with a serious expression; a red notebook lies open on the counter in the foreground. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.
